choices.english: on fleshly tablets of the heart, that is, on tablets that can feel
choices.why: αἰσθητικός, capable of perception: the living heart as against stone.

choices.english: God said somewhere, “This people draws near to Me ...” (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8–9)
choices.why: Cyril names God as the speaker; the words are Isaiah 29:13 LXX in the form Matthew 15:8–9 quotes.

[col. 332]. And indeed God said somewhere [stray numeral 5 omitted]: 'This people (λαός) draws near (ἐγγίζω) to me with their mouth (στόμα), and with their lips (χεῖλος) they honour (τιμάω) me, but their heart (καρδία) holds far off (ἀπέχω) from me; and in vain (μάτην) they revere (σέβομαι) me, teaching teachings, commandments (ἔνταλμα) of men.' But our Lord Jesus Christ on fleshly (σάρκινος) tablets (πλάξ) of heart, that is, perceptive (αἰσθητικός) ones, writes in (ἐγγράφω) for us the holy and divine laws; therefore he also said through the voice of Ezekiel the prophet: 'And I will tear out (ἐκσπάω) their stone (λίθινος) heart from their flesh and will give them a fleshly heart, so that they may walk (πορεύομαι) in my ordinances (πρόσταγμα).' If then someone has not leaned upon (προσερείδω, pf. pass.) the shadows (σκιά) through Moses, nor indeed has the law written (γράφω, pf. pass.) in ink (μέλαν) as on stone tablets, but within (ἔσω) into the mind (νοῦς) through the Spirit, this one is a letter (ἐπιστολή) of Christ known (γινώσκω, pass.) by all men. Volume 2, Discourse 1. 'And such confidence (πεποίθησις) we have through Christ toward God, etc.' Knowing [this], Paul fastens (ἀνάπτω) the dignity (ἀξίωμα) of the apostleship (ἀποστολή) not on human powers (δύναμις) but rather on the God strong (ἰσχύω) for all things and holding [it] out (ὀρέγω) to those worthy (ἄξιος) to receive [it] through Christ the mediator (μεσίτης). Therefore he says all the goods [are] to the saints in Christ; for 'from above and from the Father of the lights (φῶς) is every perfect gift (δώρημα)'; but indeed the one through whom all things and in whom all things is Christ, mediating (μεσιτεύω) [between] us and God on account of the economy (οἰκονομία), yet working (ἐνεργέω) all things from the God and Father, inasmuch as he is his very wisdom (αὐτοσοφία) and power. And what sort is the confidence through Christ toward God, hear him adding (προσεπάγω) and saying: 'Not that from ourselves we are sufficient (ἱκανός) to reckon (λογίζομαι) anything as from ourselves'; 'for all wisdom (σοφία) [is] from Lord', according to what is written; 'but our sufficiency (ἱκανότης) [is] from God, who also made us sufficient (ἱκανόω) [as] ministers (διάκονος) of a new covenant (διαθήκη), not of letter (γράμμα) but of spirit; for the letter kills (ἀποκτείνω), but the spirit makes alive (ζωοποιέω).' And what is the letter? The [col. 334] type (τύπος) in the law, the things still being fulfilled (πληρόω, pass.) as in shadows; and spirit, the power of the worship (λατρεία) in Christ, showing (ἀποφαίνω) those who approach (πρόσειμι) it through faith spiritual (πνευματικός); and by as much as the type [is] less (ἥττων) than the truth, by so much, I think, [are] those serving (διακονέω) it behind (κατόπιν) those ministering as priests (ἱερουργέω) the truth; for Christ sprinkles (ῥαντίζω) us with his own blood (αἷμα), and not for 'the purity (καθαρότης) of the flesh' only, as indeed the things in the law [did], but rather he cleanses (καθαρίζω) also 'our conscience (συνείδησις) from dead works (ἔργον)', and removes [us] from (ἐξίστημι) transgression (πλημμέλημα); and he grants (χαρίζομαι) besides this also hope (ἐλπίς) of life; for it is true that 'the one believing into the Son has eternal life'; for he has promised (ἐπαγγέλλομαι, pf.) also the resurrection (ἀνάστασις) of the very bodies and the return (ἀναφοίτησις) into incorruption (ἀφθαρσία) and into long-lasting (μακραίων) life. 'For indeed what has been glorified (δοξάζω, pf. pass.) has not been glorified in this part (μέρος), because of the surpassing (ὑπερβάλλω) glory.' He refers (ἀναφέρω) again to the incomparably (ἀσυγκρίτως) superior (ὑπερτερέω) the dignity of the divine apostleship, and having made the comparison (σύγκρισις) of the ministries (διακονία), and having very well set out (παραφέρω) the proper [mark] (ἴδιος) of each, he shows the [ministry] in Christ through spirit more radiant (διαφανής, comp.). And the aim (σκοπός) of the thought (ἔννοια) comes to him through these things, but (γεμήν) the saying (ῥητόν) has been phrased (φράζω, pf. pass.) not very clearly (σαφῶς); for it seems to be somehow not very easy to look into (εὐκάτοπτος) nor indeed ready for those wishing to see. For what [col. 335] is the 'what has been glorified has not been glorified' and what follows? It is something such as he wishes to show (δηλόω). For Moses has been glorified, he says, as minister of the law being abolished (καταργέω, pass.), but the glory of the new preaching (κήρυγμα), the [preaching] in Christ, overcoming (νικάω) the first, showed [stray numeral 6 omitted] it such as not even to seem (δοκέω) to have been glorified at all. pass_b_english: … utterly easy to throw off and very readily spat out. And indeed God said somewhere, “This people draws near to Me with their mouth and honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me; in vain do they worship Me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8–9). But our Lord Jesus Christ writes His holy and divine laws for us on fleshly tablets of the heart, that is, on tablets that can feel (2 Corinthians 3:3). That is why He also said through the voice of the prophet Ezekiel, “And I will tear out their heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in My ordinances” (Ezekiel 11:19–20). If anyone, then, does not lean on the shadows given through Moses, and does not have the law written in ink as on tablets of stone, but within, in the mind, through the Spirit, he is a letter of Christ known by all men (2 Corinthians 3:2–3).
“Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God,” and so on (2 Corinthians 3:4).

Paul, knowing it well, ascribes the dignity of the apostleship not to human powers but to God, who is mighty in all things and who holds it out, through Christ the mediator, to those worthy to receive it. That is why he says that all good things come to the saints in Christ; for “every perfect gift is from above,” from “the Father of lights” (James 1:17). Yet He through whom all things are, and in whom all things are, is Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16). He mediates between us and God in the saving economy, yet He works all things from God the Father, since He is His very Wisdom and Power (1 Corinthians 1:24).

But what is the confidence through Christ toward God? Listen as he goes on to say, “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to reckon anything as coming from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 3:5); for “all wisdom is from the Lord” (Sirach 1:1), as it is written; “but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us sufficient as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the spirit; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:5–6).

And what is the letter? The type in the law, the things still carried out as in shadows. And the spirit is the power of the worship in Christ, which shows those who approach it through faith to be spiritual. As far as the type falls short of the truth, so far, I think, do those who serve it come behind those who minister the truth as priests. For Christ sprinkles us with His own blood, and not only for “the purity of the flesh,” as the rites of the law certainly did; rather He cleanses “our conscience from dead works” (Hebrews 9:13–14) and frees us from transgression. Besides this He also grants us the hope of life; for it is true that “whoever believes in the Son has eternal life” (John 3:36). For He has promised also the resurrection of our very bodies, and their return to incorruption and to a life without end.
“For indeed what was glorified has not been glorified in this respect, because of the glory that surpasses it” (2 Corinthians 3:10).

Again he brings the dignity of the divine apostleship back to its incomparable superiority. Having compared the two ministries and set out very well what is proper to each, he shows that the ministry in Christ through the Spirit is the more radiant. This is the aim of his thought in these words, but the saying is not phrased very clearly; for it seems somehow not very easy to see into, nor ready to hand even for those who wish to see it. For what does “What was glorified has not been glorified,” and what follows, mean? What he wants to show is something like this. Moses was indeed glorified, he says, as minister of the law that is being set aside; but the glory of the new proclamation, the proclamation in Christ, overcame the first and made it seem not to have been glorified at all.
